To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) a genetic map of RFLPs has been constructed for tomato and (2) this map has been used to identify QTLs controlling quantitative traits.
the genetic dissection and the mapping of quantitative traits into discrete factors is now possible in any organism with an available linkage map of molecular markers.
we have used a complete RFLM linkage map to map QTLs controlling quantitative traits in tomato.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic dissection, mapping and cloning of QTLs for quantitative traits.
the genetic dissection and molecular characterization of quantitative traits.
the genetic control of quantitative variation in plants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic control of the quantitative trait is not a single gene, but a complex combination of many genes.

a single QTL is responsible for a significant portion of the phenotypic variation in the population under consideration, while the remaining variation is attributable to the effects of multiple QTLs, each having small individual contributions.
the genetic control of quantitative traits can be resolved by a complete linkage map.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the tomato genome contains a minimum of 15 QTLs controlling the traits we studied.
we have used the tomato genome to demonstrate a method of QTL analysis that is applicable to all higher eukaryotes.
we have shown that the Mendelian theory for quantitative traits is true.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use a linkage map to identify the genes that underlie a complex trait.
the use of a complete linkage map to study quantitative traits has become possible.
we have demonstrated that it is possible to use the complete genome of tomato to map QTLs for quantitative traits.
